analysis.one_liner: Requires all employers to provide earned paid sick leave, plus 14 emergency days during public health crises.
analysis.headline: Introduced days before COVID-19 shut down the country, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every employer — from a one-person shop to the largest corporation, plus governments and Congress itself — to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (7 days) a year. If a public health emergency is declared, every worker would immediately get up to 14 more paid days off, usable for their own illness, a sick family member, a closed workplace or school, or dealing with domestic violence. Workers could use the time without losing pay, and employers could not fire or penalize them for taking it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without paid sick leave, who are disproportionately low-wage, hourly, and service-sector employees. They could stay home when sick or when exposed to a contagious disease instead of working sick, and could take paid leave to care for a sick child or family member, including when schools or workplaces close during an emergency. Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking could take paid time for medical care, counseling, relocation, or court proceedings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly and low-wage workers without sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Every employer with at least one employee must provide 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (7 days) per year, and the time carries over year to year [S2] [S3].

When a public health emergency is declared, each worker immediately gets up to 14 additional paid days off, usable the day the emergency is declared regardless of how long they have been employed — no waiting period [S2] [S3].

The leave covers the worker's own illness or medical care, caring for a sick child, spouse, parent, or domestic partner, a workplace or school closed by a public health emergency, exposure to a communicable disease even without infection, and absences related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking [S3].

Employers may not fire, demote, or retaliate against a worker for using the leave, may not count it against attendance policies, and may not require the worker to find a replacement before taking it [S3].
No doctor's note or other documentation can be required during a public health emergency, so workers can use the time during exactly the moment when clinics are overwhelmed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — private businesses of any size, public agencies, and congressional offices — would pay the wages for sick time taken, and would bear administrative costs for recordkeeping and posting notices. Employers with already-generous leave policies would owe nothing beyond what they provide.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to every employer with at least one employee and takes effect immediately on enactment, so businesses would absorb wage costs for leave with no phase-in or small-business exemption [S3].

In a public health emergency, up to 14 days of paid leave must be available immediately with no certification from a health care provider, which employers could see as open to misuse and difficult to schedule around [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the cost lands on employers who may respond by slowing hiring, cutting hours, or raising prices, and that businesses whose margins are thin would feel it most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial for the roughly one-quarter of the workforce that lacked any paid sick leave when this was introduced — the difference between staying home with a contagious illness and working sick, or between income and nothing when a child's school closes. The cost is real but bounded: 7 days a year earned by hours actually worked, and employers who already offer equivalent leave owe nothing extra. The immediate 14-day emergency entitlement with no documentation requirement is the most aggressive part and the likeliest friction point with employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Patty Murray introduced the bill on March 5, 2020, with five original cosponsors including the Senate Democratic leader [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the full Senate never considered the bill [S5].
The bill had 24 cosponsors, 23 Democrats and 1 Independent, and no Republican support [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without ever leaving committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the cost of providing paid sick leave to every worker are better off because the bill never moved. Weeks after it was introduced, Congress passed a narrower emergency law that gave some workers two weeks of paid sick leave related to COVID-19 but exempted large employers and let small employers opt out — a far smaller obligation than this bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have funded the leave

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucused with them; not a single Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with hourly, low-wage workforces (retail, food service, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: These employers are the least likely to already offer paid sick leave, so they would bear the full new wage cost. Their interest in defeating the bill ran directly against the workers who most needed the leave.

Unlike the narrow COVID law Congress passed weeks later, this bill had no small-business exemption and took effect immediately, so small employers would pay the same wage costs as large ones. Their workers, however, would gain the same protections.

industries.industry: Public agencies and state and local governments
industries.note: The bill covers public agencies as employers, and it waives state sovereign immunity for employee suits when states accept federal funds, so governments would owe paid sick time and face liability for violations.
